en.title: The Echo Chamber: Marinelli and Vikander Ignite Venice with Raw Addiction Drama
en.summary: A powerful, unfinished screenplay from Bernardo Bertolucci finds new life in Andrea Pallaoro's haunting drama. Luca Marinelli and Alicia Vikander deliver career-defining performances as a couple grappling with addiction and its devastating fallout.
en.body:
## A Ghost in the Machine

Venice has been set ablaze, not by fireworks, but by the searing intensity of **Andrea Pallaoro**'s **The Echo Chamber**. Piloting an unfinished screenplay by the legendary **Bernardo Bertolucci**, Pallaoro and his co-writers **Ilaria Bernardini** and **Ludovica Rampoldi** have crafted a film that feels both deeply personal and universally resonant. While the spectral influence of Bertolucci is present in the intimate dialogue and realist restraint, Pallaoro’s distinct directorial hand is undeniable. His signature long, still shots create an almost unbearable tension, allowing the unspoken conflicts within the characters to simmer and boil. The film opens with a jolt: **Luca Marinelli** as Leo, a renowned record producer, revels in a moment of drug-fueled euphoria, a stark contrast to the somber tone that follows. His partner, Anne, played by **Alicia Vikander**, walks in, initially surprised but quickly drawn into his tender, narcotized passion. This fleeting burst of inebriated energy is the film's only glimpse of unbridled loudness, a deliberate choice that makes the subsequent unraveling all the more devastating.

> "My own destruction might be exactly what I want." – Leo

The narrative quickly pivots from this explosive beginning to a more pensive exploration of addiction's grueling toll. Leo’s overdose in Anne’s lap sets the stage for a drama steeped in soft, bitter introspection. Anne, a physiotherapist, initially met Leo when she began treating him for chronic back pain, a relationship that becomes tragically entangled with his growing opioid dependence. As the film unfolds through flashbacks, we witness the slow erosion of their bond, the lines between intimacy, dependence, care, and control blurring into an unrecognizable mess.

## The Sound of Silence and Song

**The Echo Chamber** resonated so powerfully at Venice that it was met with an impressive eight-minute standing ovation, a testament to its emotional heft and the electrifying chemistry between its leads. **Luca Marinelli** and **Alicia Vikander** are nothing short of spectacular, turning in two of the finest performances of their careers. Marinelli embodies Leo’s struggle with a raw vulnerability, while Vikander’s Anne navigates the complex terrain of a partner caught between love and the devastating consequences of addiction. The film also features a remarkable turn from **Susan Sarandon**, whose presence adds another layer of poignant depth. Her singing, on original songs by **Clément Ducol** and **Émilie Gassin**, is imbued with a lovely, unforced sense of broody introspection and yearning, creating charged scenes that balance honesty and self-protection. Each subtle shift in body language and gaze between the actors conveys lifetimes of unspoken emotion, making this a deeply affecting cinematic experience for fans of character-driven dramas and powerful performances alike.

## What's Next

While specific release dates for **The Echo Chamber** are still being finalized, its triumphant premiere at Venice suggests a wide theatrical release is on the horizon. Audiences worldwide are eagerly awaiting the chance to experience this intense and beautifully crafted drama for themselves.

content_raw: “My own destruction might be exactly what I want.” – Leo Italian cinema maestro Bernardo Bertolucci died in 2018, leaving behind one unfinished screenplay. For his fourth feature, burgeoning Italian writer-director Andrea Pallaoro was given the keys to that coveted, unfinished script. Pallaoro finished writing the screenplay alongside Bertolucci’s original co-writers, Ilaria Bernardini and Ludovica Rampoldi, before he took the reins. The Echo Chamber doesn’t feel or play like a Bertolucci film. His spectre is there in the dialogue, the scenario, and the realist restraint. But Pallaoro brings his distinct style to the homebody story, one traced through long, still, quiet shots that hold the unspoken tension of the frame and the messy conflicts within. In a ritzy flat in London, the film opens with a bang: renowned record producer Leo (Luca Marinelli) lines up crisp streaks of white powder to snort while he bounces around to blasting club music, the likes of which he doesn’t produce. Anne (Alicia Vikander) walks through the door, surprised to see Leo in such a state but swept into a second-hand high by his tender, narcotized romantic passion almost immediately. We don’t experience that high level of energy for the rest of the film. It’s the only glimpse of inebriated euphoria—and loudness—we get from Leo’s addict phase, and it’s an affecting move for Pallaoro to start there out of context. He shows us something seemingly innocuous, then slowly unpacks the grueling affliction and pain associated with it, both for Leo and Anne. The scene ends quickly with Leo overdosing in Anne’s lap, and the severe stakes of the soft, bitter, pensive drama set in.  Anne, a physiotherapist, meets Leo, a victim of chronic back pain, when she starts making clinical calls to his flat, acting as both masseuse and doctor. It doesn’t take long for the lovebirds to fall head-over-heels for each other, and it takes even less time for that love to become codependent obsession, a floating metaphor for the substance abuse to come. The muscle therapy and massages only do so much, so Anne prescribes Leo opioids for the pain. One life-threatening addiction later, she’s drowning in the guilt of having introduced him to his potential end.  All of this happens in the process of Leo recording an album with the sultry (fictional) great Ava May (Susan Sarandon, who Pallaoro is smart to bring back into the songstress spotlight, where she blossomed with The Rocky Horror Picture Show in 1975), who occupies a dark, hushed, smoky singer-songwriter territory. But he has to put the record on hold to go to rehab, during which Leo and Anne never see each other. However, they’re constantly walking in the other’s wake. Anne lurks around his apartment while he’s at rehab—to smell him, to touch the things he touched, to feel some kind of phantom connection. Eventually, Leo realizes she’s doing it.
